Suvela Mountain; Sarama Comforts Sita

Stories from the Ramayana

Suvela Mountain; Sarama Comforts Sita

Sita is shown an illusory head — and Sarama tells her the truth

In everyday English — Yuddha Kanda, sargas 31–35, 47–48

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, as if you are sitting with everyone at home.

This book is two fears — and two reassurances. First Ravana frightens Sita, then Sarama comforts her. Then comes the fear of the serpent-arrows, and Trijata comforts her. Where there is fear, read slowly; where comfort comes, let warmth into your voice.

The yellow boxes hold the characters' own words. Change your voice a little as you speak them — Ravana furious, Sita sorrowing, Sarama soft and steady.

(Purple hints) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

The green box at the end of each part — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listeners speak.

The main story of this book is Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, sargas 31–35 and 47–48 — the army's camp on Mount Suvela, the illusory head, Sarama's comfort, and Trijata's comfort after the serpent-arrows. Anything more you may want to know is given separately at the end, in Where This Story Comes From.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Rama — prince of Ayodhya, archer. Warm dark-brown skin, fully clothed, barefoot in the forest. With his vanara army he has crossed the ocean and stands before Lanka.

Lakshmana — Rama's younger brother, beside him at every step. Bow in hand, like Rama, a little lighter in complexion.

Sita — held captive in the Ashoka grove. Wheat-gold skin, long black braid with white jasmine flowers, small gold jhumka earrings, a thin gold nose-ring on her left nostril, a single pale saree, no crown.

Ravana — king of Lanka. Tall, dark-complexioned, black moustache, tall golden crown, a single head, royal robes.

Sarama — wife of Vibhishana, Sita's friend. She comes and goes in the grove and tells Sita the truth.

Trijata — an elderly rakshasi woman who guards Sita, but whose heart is on Sita's side.

Vidyujjihva — a rakshasa skilled in illusion, who can fashion anything by maya.

Indrajit — Ravana's eldest son, also called Meghanada. Blessed with the power to fight unseen.

Sugriva — king of the vanaras, Rama's friend and commander.

Vibhishana — Ravana's younger brother, who took shelter with Rama for the sake of dharma. Sarama is his wife.

1 · The Army Camps on Suvela · · THE ARMY CAMPS ON SUVELA

The bridge across the ocean was built. The vanara army — lakhs upon lakhs of vanaras — crossed the bridge and stepped onto the soil of Lanka.

Rama halted the army at the foot of Mount Suvela. Suvela — the great mountain standing before Lanka, from which the city of Lanka could be seen clearly.

Rama climbed the mountain with Sugriva, Jambavan and his captains. From above they saw Lanka — golden gates, tall palaces, waving flags, a deep moat and strong walls all around.

Ravana too had climbed to the roof of his palace. From there he saw the army — the vanara host spread all the way to the shore of the sea, with no end in sight.

Ravana said to his ministers — “Look, what an army has come! But Lanka cannot be breached — these vanaras will never break its walls.”

Down on Suvela, Rama said to his captains — “Lanka is strong. We must lay siege to it with thought and care.”

Both sides were ready. The war had not yet begun — but the sound of war was already in the air.

Pause and think — Rama looks at Lanka from above, Ravana looks at the army from above — each is watching the other. Is watching the enemy before a war also part of the war? And Mount Suvela — is seeing from a high place different from seeing from below?

2 · Ravana's New Trick · · RAVANA'S NEW TRICK

Ravana knew — fighting the army would be hard. So he thought of another trick — one that needed no sword, no army.

He summoned Vidyujjihva — the rakshasa who knew illusion, who could fashion anything by maya.

Ravana said — “Fashion Rama's head by illusion — and his bow too. Make it so that whoever sees it takes it for real.”

Vidyujjihva said — “As you command, my king.” — and by maya he fashioned Rama's head and his bow.

Ravana lifted the illusory head and the bow — and set out for the Ashoka grove. One thought was in his mind — break Sita, and Rama will break too.

Sita sat beneath the Ashoka tree in the grove — waiting for Rama, chanting Rama's name.

Pause and think — Ravana wants to fight not with a sword but with a lie. Can a lie also be a weapon? And when someone wants to defeat truth with a lie — whom does he fear — Rama, or the truth itself?

3 · The Illusory Head · · THE ILLUSORY HEAD

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it speaks of a death shown by trickery. Elders, please read it gently.

Ravana came into the grove — carrying the illusory head and the bow. He placed them before Sita.

Ravana said — “Look, Sita! Your Rama is slain. In the night, as he slept, my general Prahasta killed him. Here is his head — and here is his bow.”

Sita looked — and her heart trembled. She felt — Rama truly is no more.

She began to weep — “Alas, Rama! You have gone? What shall I do without you?” — she sank to the earth, tears flowing from her eyes.

Ravana went away laughing. He thought — the trick has worked.

But one thought stayed in Sita's mind — this head does not feel real. How could anyone kill Rama as he slept? And Rama's bow — would it just lie there like that?

Pause and think — What Sita saw was not real — but her sorrow was real. Can something seen with one's own eyes still be false? And when doubt rises in the mind — that this is not real — where does that doubt come from?

4 · Sarama Comes · · SARAMA COMES

Sita was weeping — then Sarama came. Sarama — wife of Vibhishana — was Sita's friend in the grove. She sat quietly beside Sita.

Sarama said softly — “Sita, do not weep. What you saw is not real — it is maya.”

Sita asked — “Maya? But I saw it with my own eyes!”

Sarama said — “Ravana had Vidyujjihva weave an illusion. Rama is alive — he is camped on Mount Suvela with his army. I myself have heard the noise of the vanaras.”

Sarama told her — “Rama has crossed the ocean. His army stands before Lanka. Ravana wants to frighten you into giving up hope — but do not be afraid.”

Sita's tears stopped. Hope returned to her heart — Rama is alive! Rama has come!

Sita said — “Sarama, you have saved my heart. You are a friend — and a friend of truth.”

Pause and think — Sarama told Sita the truth — and the truth lightened her sorrow. Is telling the truth also a kind of service? And when someone is afraid — what does it take to tell them the truth — courage, or love?

5 · The Serpent Arrows · · THE SERPENT ARROWS

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it speaks of Rama and Lakshmana falling unconscious. Elders, please read it gently.

The war had begun. Arrows flew from both sides — vanaras fought lifting boulders and trees, rakshasas rode in chariots.

Then came Ravana's son Indrajit — fighting unseen. He had the boon that he could fight hidden. No one could see him — only his arrows could be seen.

He loosed the Nagastra — serpent-arrows. The arrows fell from the sky as serpents — and coiled around Rama and Lakshmana. The serpents wrapped both brothers — and both fell to the earth.

The vanaras panicked — “Rama has fallen! Lakshmana has fallen!” — Sugriva and Jambavan ran up — but the two brothers did not stir.

When Ravana heard this, he laughed. He thought — the war is won. Now show Sita — that her Ramas have fallen.

Pause and think — Indrajit could not be seen — only his arrows could be seen. Is fighting hidden an act of valour? And when both brothers fell — what were the vanaras afraid of — Rama's defeat, or their own hope breaking?

6 · Sita in the Flying Chariot · · SITA IN THE FLYING CHARIOT

Ravana seated Sita in the Pushpaka vimana — the flying chariot that travels through the sky. Trijata was seated with her too.

Ravana said — “Come, Sita — look at your Rama. He lies on the battlefield — bound by serpents. Now accept it — you have no support left.”

The vimana rose into the sky — and passed over the battlefield. Below, Sita saw — Rama and Lakshmana lying on the earth, wrapped in serpents.

Sita's heart trembled again — “Can it be that Rama truly…?” — she began to weep.

But Trijata took her hand — “Wait, Sita. First look — then weep.”

Pause and think — Ravana takes Sita in the vimana — so that she may see defeat with her own eyes. Is showing someone a defeat also a trick? And Trijata says — first look, then weep — does weeping before looking cloud the truth?

7 · Trijata's Reassurance · · TRIJATA'S REASSURANCE

Trijata said to Sita — “Look, Sita — look carefully. Rama and Lakshmana are not dead.”

Trijata said — “Their faces still shine — the face of the dead is not like this. They are breathing — their chests rise and fall.”

“And look — the vanaras stand beside them, guarding them. If they had died, the vanaras would not stand so calm — they would weep and wail.”

“Serpents can bind them — but they cannot kill them. They will rise, Sita — they will surely rise.”

Sita looked carefully — it was true! Rama's face was calm — as if he were asleep. His chest rose slowly — he was breathing.

Sita's tears stopped. She said — “Trijata, you speak truly. Rama is alive — he will rise.”

The vimana returned — Sita sat again in the grove — but this time there was trust in her heart.

Pause and think — Trijata taught Sita how to look — look at the face, look at the breath, look at the vanaras. Is looking alone enough to recognise the truth — or is patience also needed? And when someone gives us trust — what does that trust rest on — words, or seeing?

8 · Hope at Dawn · · HOPE AT DAWN

The night passed. Morning came — the first ray of the sun fell on Mount Suvela.

Sita sat in the grove — among the Ashoka blossoms. There was no fear in her heart now — there was hope.

Twice Ravana had tried to break her — with the illusory head, and by showing her the serpent-arrows. Twice someone had saved her by telling her the truth — once Sarama, once Trijata.

Down on the battlefield Rama and Lakshmana still lay bound by serpents — but Trijata's words echoed in Sita's ears — “They will rise, Sita — they will surely rise.”

But that story — is in the next book.

Pause and think — Sita broke twice — and rose twice. Is breaking itself defeat — or is rising itself victory? And Sarama and Trijata — two different women, twice giving trust — is the one who gives trust the greatest support of all?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main Source

The main story of this book is Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, sargas 31–35 and 47–48.

Mount Suvela — Sarga 31

The army halting at the foot of Mount Suvela; Rama climbing the mountain with his captains to look at Lanka; Ravana looking at the vanara army from his palace roof — this is in sarga 31.

The Illusory Head — Sargas 33–34

Ravana having Vidyujjihva fashion an illusory head and bow by maya; placing them before Sita and saying that Prahasta killed Rama in the night as he slept; Sita's lament — this is in sargas 33–34.

Sarama's Reassurance — Sarga 35

Sarama, wife of Vibhishana, telling Sita that the head is maya, that Rama is alive and camped on Suvela with his army — this is in sarga 35.

The Serpent-Arrows — Sarga 47

Indrajit fighting unseen and loosing the Nagastra; Rama and Lakshmana falling bound by serpents; Ravana taking Sita in the Pushpaka vimana to show them to her — this is in sarga 47.

Trijata's Reassurance — Sarga 48

Trijata telling Sita that the two brothers are alive — their faces still shine, they are breathing, the vanaras guard them — this is in sarga 48.

About the Pictures

In this book the illusory head is never shown as a bloody or severed thing — it is shown as an illusion dissolving into golden mist and flowers. The serpent-arrow picture too has no blood or wounds — Rama and Lakshmana lie still, as if asleep. The fear is told only in words.

What Happens Next

How Rama and Lakshmana are freed from the serpents — the coming of Garuda — is told in the next book of this series.
